title: Data Transformations
story: The old system stores temperatures as integers (25, 30, 18), but the new dashboard displays words ('warm', 'hot', 'cool'). The database has student IDs mapped to names, but the report needs a flat list. Data rarely arrives in the format you need — transformation is the bridge.
why: Real-world programming is mostly data transformation — converting between formats, reshaping collections, and mapping types — these patterns appear in every application you'll ever build.
analogy: Data transformation is like translating a book — the story (data) stays the same, but the language (format) changes. English to Spanish is like Int to Str; a dictionary to a list of definitions is like Map to Vec.
try_it: Write `transform_in_reverse` — given a Vec[Str] of words, convert back to Vec[Int] by word length. Then write `map_values_to_vec` that extracts just the values from a Map into a Vec (ignoring keys). Chain a transformation: Vec of numbers to Vec of words to filtered 'hot' entries to count. Print results at each stage.
tips: Each transformation function does ONE conversion — don't combine number-to-word and filtering in one function
When converting Map to Vec, you need a separate Vec of keys since Map has no guaranteed iteration order
Transform functions always return new collections — never modify the input
common_mistakes: Converting Map values without handling missing keys — `.get(&key)` returns Option, always match it
Mixing transformation logic with business logic — keep the 'what' (ranges) separate from the 'how' (iteration)
Forgetting that Vec[Int] and Vec[Str] are completely different types — you can't assign one to the other
